paper_title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: LLM agents solve long-horizon tasks through sequences of decisions and environment interactions [30, 36]. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) trains these agents using outcome feedback, such as whether code change passes test suite. Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) assigns advantages by comparing rewards within group of trajectories sampled for the same task [26]. With binary outcome rewards, group in which every trajectory fails has zero reward variation and provides no reward-based policy gradient. We refer to this case as an all-fail group. Such group leaves the policy without successful trajectory to reinforce, even when some intermediate decisions could support successful continuation. External guidance offers direct way to recover learning signals from all-fail groups by introducing successful behaviors that the current policy rarely generates. Existing methods for GRPO often derive such guidance from complete task-level solutions [16, 29, 34]. This choice treats complete solution as the source of guidance. For long-horizon agents, however, failure may be localized: short corrective segment can lead to state from which the current policy can complete the remaining task. Thus, using complete solutions in this long-horizon setting incurs both computational and distributional costs. 1 complete long-horizon trajectory may span tens or hundreds of interaction turns (e.g., Qwen3.5-9B rollouts on our SWE tasks average 83.7 agent turns). Repeatedly generating such trajectories with strong proposal model requires expensive inference. The proposal model is requested even for decisions that the current policy can already make. Also, using long pre-collected trajectories as supervision exposes the learner to off-policy risk, increasing the mismatch between the training distribution and the current policys behavior [15, 23, 24]. These costs pose two design problems. The first is allocating proposal-model computation to bottlenecks encountered by current policy. The second is converting local proposals into training target that reflects the current policys ability to complete the task after each proposal. We address both problems with SPLICE, which introduces failure-localized option splicing with current-policy continuation evaluation. For an all-fail group, proposal model selects splice point in one current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options. We splice each option at this point, return control to the current policy, and sample repeated continuations to task completion. Their terminal outcomes estimate the options current-policy continuation value, and we convert the positive values into return-weighted local target. Only all-fail groups enter this splice branch, while other groups continue with standard GRPO. The bounded options save expensive proposal-model inference, while anchoring them in current-policy history and supervising on the local target limits off-policy exposure. We evaluate SPLICE on Software Engineering and Deep Research tasks. Across SWE-bench Verified and BrowseComp-Plus, it improves GRPO by 2.89.8 percentage points. On fixed set of initially failed SWE tasks, it raises graduation rate from 8.1% to 18.9%. SPLICE uses fewer proposal-model rollout turns than fulltrajectory guidance baselines while achieving better performance. Extensive experiments show that SPLICE can recover all-fail tasks without requiring the proposal model to generate or supervise complete trajectories. Our contributions are as follows: (1) We introduce SPLICE, which formulates recovery from all-fail groups in long-horizon agent RL as learner-conditioned option splicing. This formulation allocates costly proposalmodel computation only to splice points selected online. (2) We use current-policy continuation returns to define target distribution over proposed options. By splicing bounded options into current-policy histories and fitting to this local distribution online, the update limits off-policy exposure relative to full-trajectory guidance. (3) We show across Software Engineering and Deep Research tasks that SPLICE improves performance and recovery of initially failed tasks while reducing proposal-model cost.

sections.title: 2.1 Agentic RL and All-Fail Groups
sections.content: Reinforcement learning has been extended from single-response reasoning to agents that act over multiple turns in stateful environments [28, 30]. These settings often use sparse trajectory-level rewards from executable verifiers, which allow policy optimization over complete sequences of reasoning, actions, and environment observations. GRPO samples group of trajectories for the same task and estimates each advantage from its return relative to the group, avoiding learned value model [5, 26]. The resulting update depends on reward variation among trajectories sampled from the same task. Under binary outcome rewards, an all-fail group has zero reward for every trajectory, so its reward-relative advantages vanish. All-fail groups contain no positive trajectory to reinforce, making exploration on hard tasks the central problem. Existing methods reallocate sampling or filter zero-variance groups [32, 35], construct advantages from failed responses [13], or revise failures using gold answers [8]. External guidance offers another route by proposing behaviors that the current policy rarely samples, which we review below.

sections.title: 2.2 External Guidance in RL
sections.content: One line of work conditions RL rollouts on precomputed hints or prefixes, while optimizing only the policygenerated continuation [11, 18, 20, 25, 31, 34]. Another line trains directly on complete external solutions through supervised, off-policy, or mixed-policy objectives [7, 16, 29, 33]. Such guidance is often derived from expert solutions, while direct supervision requires complete expert trajectories. Generating these trajectories is expensive for long-horizon agents, and expert-induced histories can differ from those visited by the current 2 policy, creating covariate shift and compounding errors [15, 23]. Concurrent work RSTG combines GRPO with on-policy distillation (OPD) on teacher solutions for all-fail groups [9], requiring aligned teacher and student token spaces. SPLICE instead queries proposal model online for short options at selected splice points in current-policy trajectories. Learner-conditioned continuation evaluation and local supervision reduce proposal-model cost and limit off-policy exposure.

sections.title: 4 Method
sections.content: Overview. SPLICE supplements GRPO with splice update for all-fail groups. Given an all-fail group, proposal model πρ selects an intermediate point in one failed trajectory and generates bounded options after resuming the interaction from that point. We splice each option at this point and evaluate it with continuations sampled from πold. We then retain options with positive estimated return and fit πθ to their return-weighted distribution. Figure 1 summarizes this process. Update routing. (3) Mixed-reward groups use Equation 2, all-success groups are skipped, and all-fail groups enter the Splice branch described below.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Tasks and data. For Software Engineering (SWE), we combine subsets of SWE-Gym [19] and R2EGym [10], excluding tasks from repositories that overlap with SWE-bench. We evaluate resolve rate on SWE-bench Verified [12]. For Deep Research, we use dataset curated from open-source datasets with quality-control pipeline, which Appendix B.2 describes. We evaluate answer accuracy on BrowseCompPlus [1], using Qwen3-Embedding-8B as the retriever and gpt-oss-20b as the judge model. To give all methods access to the same amount and distribution of training data, we sample fixed subset of 3,200 tasks for both SWE and Deep Research. We report SWE and Deep Research performance in the main results, and further analyses use SWE. Models. We study two policy families based on Qwen3-8B [21] and Qwen3.5-9B [22]. Our Qwen3-8B experiments use shared cold-start checkpoint to adapt to the scaffold interfaces and tool-call formats, denoted Qwen3-8B-CS, whereas Qwen3.5-9B starts directly from its released checkpoint. Cold-start details are in Appendix C. Thinking is disabled for Qwen3-8B-CS for better performance, and is enabled for Qwen3.59B. We use Qwen3.5-122B-A10B as the proposal model for both policy families. We report main results for both families, and further analyses use Qwen3-8B-CS as the current policy. Agent scaffolds. For SWE, we use OpenHands [27] as the scaffold. We keep the default system prompt and tools unchanged. For Deep Research, we customize the scaffold on Uni-Agent [4], providing three tools, search, open, and find. For all training methods, the turn limit is 150 and the context limit is 128k tokens. Training configuration. Unless varied in ablations, we use = 3 proposed options and = 3 currentpolicy continuations per option. The adaptive option horizon uses α = 0.3 in Equation 4. We record eligible splice points every = 4 agent turns. The default SWE implementation restores container snapshots, while Deep Research stores only the interaction history. Appendix reports the hardware allocation and other hyperparameters. Reporting Convention. We report mean sample standard deviation (SD) across three runs. We evaluate the final checkpoint from every training run. Comparison Setup. We consider SPLICE, SFT, RL, SFT+RL, and ReLIFT, starting from the same initial policy and using the common 3,200-task subset for each task domain. This protocol controls the available task data rather than method-specific computation, which we compare separately in Section 5.4. For SFT, the proposal model generates one full trajectory for every task in the common subset, and rejection sampling retains only successful trajectories for supervised fine-tuning. RL applies GRPO directly to the initial policy. SFT+RL initializes from the resulting SFT checkpoint and runs GRPO for the same number of RL steps as SPLICE. We adapt ReLIFT [16] to the online setting by requesting one full proposal-model trajectory for each task with an all-fail group and adding it to the buffer only upon verified success. Following the original method, ReLIFT triggers fine-tuning step when the buffer contains at least 64 examples.

sections.title: 5.2 Main Results
sections.content: Table 1 first shows the limitation of applying RL directly to the initial policy. RL improves performance in all four settings, but the gains over the initial policy are limited to 3.75.2 percentage points. This modest improvement is consistent with the sparse-reward exploration bottleneck: GRPO can reinforce sampled successes but obtains no reward-based gradient from all-fail groups. Providing successful trajectories before RL yields substantially stronger results. SFT+RL outperforms direct RL by 1.58.5 points across the four settings, while the RL stage improves its SFT initialization by further 1.22.9 points. These results show that RL achieves better performance after SFT has exposed the policy to successful task trajectories. Online external guidance offers an alternative way to supply successful behavior during RL. ReLIFT improves over direct RL by 0.73.8 points, showing that online guidance improves final performance in this comparison. SPLICE improves further over ReLIFT by 2.16.0 points and exceeds the higher-compute SFT+RL baseline 6 Table 1 Main results on SWE-bench Verified and BrowseComp-Plus. These comparisons support the use of learner-conditioned local options rather than complete proposal trajectories for external guidance.

sections.title: 5.3 Recovering Failed Tasks
sections.content: We assess whether proposal guidance helps recover failed tasks and examine how training gains vary with task difficulty. Proposal Hit and Graduation Rates. The proposal hit rate is the fraction of proposal attempts on SWE training tasks that yield at least one verified successful trajectory. The graduation rate is the fraction of initially failed SWE training tasks solved by the trained policy. We evaluate each trained method with one rollout per task, and task graduates if this rollout succeeds. Table 2 Recovery and proposal-model cost on SWE training tasks. Proposal hit and graduation rates are percentages. Method RL ReLIFT SPLICE Proposal hit Graduation πρ Turns (k) N/A 55.12.1 30.70.5 8.11.1 15.91.0 18.90.3 0.00.0 113.45.9 93.52.6 As shown in Table 2, SPLICE obtains proposal hit rate of 30.7%, 24.4 percentage points below ReLIFT, while using 17.5% fewer proposal-model turns. Despite the lower hit rate, SPLICE graduates 18.9% of the initial-failure set, compared with 15.9% for ReLIFT and 8.1% for RL. The gains of 3.0 points over ReLIFT and 10.8 points over RL show that the splice updates yield stronger recovery in this experiment. Recovery Across Task Difficulty. We compare training gains against standard GRPO across fixed Easy, Medium, and Hard subsets of the 3,200-task SWE training set; Appendix defines the partition. sections.title: 5.4 Training Dynamics and Cost
sections.content: We analyze training along three complementary axes: resolve-rate dynamics over training updates, proposalmodel rollout turns, and total wall-clock time. Proposal-model turns isolate generation by the expensive guidance model, whereas wall-clock time measures end-to-end training cost. Fig. 2 Training dynamics and cost. (a) Resolve rate every 10 RL steps. (b,c) Resolve rate versus proposal-model turns and total wall-clock time, respectively. Higher and further left is better. Training Dynamics. Figure 2(a) compares how resolve rate changes during training. RL improves quickly but later fluctuates at relatively low level. ReLIFT improves over longer horizon, while SPLICE shows no early advantage but later surpasses both baselines. Thus, external guidance supports continued improvement, with SPLICE achieving the strongest late-stage performance. Proposal-Model and Wall-Clock Cost. Figure 2(b,c) compares proposal-model generation and end-toend training time. SFT collects complete proposal-model trajectory for every task, giving it the highest proposal-model cost and longest runtime, whereas RL uses no proposal model and finishes fastest. ReLIFT and SPLICE spend additional time on online external guidance but outperform RL. For both methods, we asynchronously generate rollout batches for RL and supervised updates with staleness = 2 and observe comparable resolve rates to synchronous training; Appendix provides configuration details. SPLICE requests only bounded proposal options rather than complete trajectories; despite the additional student continuations used to evaluate them, it requires less proposal-model computation and wall-clock time than ReLIFT and SFT while achieving the highest resolve rate.

sections.title: 5.5 Mechanism and Ablation Studies
sections.content: We test four design choices: how continuation outcomes define the local target, which policy generates the continuations, how much of each proposal-generated branch enters the loss, and how long each option should be. All variants are trained under the same setting, except for the changes stated in each comparison. Resolve measures SWE-bench Verified performance; Graduation and Hit are training-set metrics defined in Section 5.3. Appendix studies strategies for selecting splice points. Continuation Evaluation and Target Construction. We compare SPLICEs return-weighted target with three alternatives. Single option directly supervises one generated option without further verification. Hard top- (cid:98)Q retains = = 3 continuation evaluation but places all target mass on the option attaining the largest positive (cid:98)Qk. We randomly select one if multiple options have the same (cid:98)Qk. Uniform positive 8 uses the same continuation outcomes but assigns equal weight to every option with (cid:98)Qk > 0. SPLICE improves Resolve by 4.5 points and Graduation by 6.6 points over single-option supervision. More directly, it exceeds hard top- (cid:98)Q by 1.4 Resolve points and 1.2 Graduation points under matched proposal and continuation budgets. This result supports retaining soft distribution over verified alternatives rather than collapsing the target onto the best. Relative to uniform positive, return-dependent weighting adds 2.0 Resolve points and 1.8 Graduation points, showing that the relative continuation returns provide useful information beyond binary outcome filtering. We first replace current-policy continuations with proposal-model continuations while retaining supervision only on the bounded options. This change improves Resolve from 25.7% to 26.2% and Graduation from 18.9% to 19.4%, but raises proposal-model rollout turns from 93.5k to 372.5k, or 4.0 as many turns. The full-suffix variant also supervises the action tokens in successful proposal-generated continuations. To control the contribution of sequence length, we average the token loss within each branch and then average successful branches within each option before applying its target weight. Full-suffix supervision lowers both Resolve and Graduation while using 365.9k proposal-model turns. The two variants therefore use comparable proposal-model computation, but extending supervision to the successful suffix degrades performance. This may be attributed to greater off-policy exposure along proposal-induced histories and accumulated covariate shift in long trajectories. Adaptive Option Horizon. We vary the fraction in Equation 4 over α {0.1, 0.3, 0.5}, with α = 0.3 as the reference. Reducing α to 0.1 cuts proposal-model turns from 93.5k to 33.7k, 64.0% reduction, but lowers Hit, Resolve and Graduation. This pattern suggests that very short options are less likely to reach state from which the current policy can complete the task. Increasing α to 0.5 raises Hit by 2.3 points and proposal-model turns from 93.5k to 157.0k, 67.9% increase. Resolve and Graduation nevertheless slightly decrease. Longer teacher options therefore do not yield better proposal-free policy in this comparison.

sections.title: 5.6 Case Study: Redirecting an Incomplete Repair
sections.content: We illustrate the splice update with SWE-Gym instance dask__dask-10506 in Figure 3, which concerns division-by-zero error when writing an empty array to Zarr. The raw steps are summarized for clarity. An Incomplete Repair. We randomly select one trajectory in this all-fail group. It passes 471 existing regression tests and one of the two issue-specific tests, but fails test_load_store_chunk. In this trajectory, 9 Fig. 3 case sampled from training with summarized trajectory steps. (a) Recorded actions and verifier feedback from failed rollout. (b) Options from the proposal model, followed by current-policy continuations. the agent reproduces the exception, inspects the shared write helper, and then changes Zarr chunk sizes from zero to one. This change fixes the reported example, but the helper still attempts to write empty blocks when called directly. Option Splicing and Verification. The proposal model selects the branchable point after 20 completed turns, before the first production edit. All three options begin from this point. After each option, the current policy produces three independent continuations. The returns are (0, 0, 0), (1, 0, 0), and (1, 1, 1) for ω1, ω2, and ω3, respectively. Thus, the diagnostic option sometimes leads the current policy to the complete repair. These give (cid:98)Q = (0, 1 3 , 1): the API-only option is discarded, while the diagnostic and guarded-write options remain. Equations 67 assign the retained options weights of approximately 0.12 and 0.88. The resulting target favors the guarded helper repair while retaining some probability on the diagnostic behavior that may also support successful completion. This example illustrates how short, outcome-verified alternatives can extract local training target from an all-fail group.

sections.title: 6 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.content: Limitations. SPLICE introduces current-policy rollout computation because each option is evaluated through multiple continuations. Our asynchronous pipeline adds limited wall-clock time in our experiments, but the cost may be larger in environments with expensive execution. Also, estimating each option value Increasing its accuracy requires more current-policy from three continuations introduces sampling error. continuations or stronger model, creating trade-off between estimation quality and inference cost. Conclusion. We introduced SPLICE, training method that recovers learning signals from all-fail rollout groups in long-horizon agent RL. It splices bounded proposal-model options into failed current-policy trajectories online. We evaluate each option through current-policy continuations and train on the resulting return-weighted local target. Replacing complete proposal trajectories with local options online reduces proposal-model cost and limits off-policy exposure and covariate shift. Across two policy families and two agent tasks, SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance, with particularly strong recovery on initially failed tasks.

sections.title: B Training Data
sections.content: B.1 Software Engineering We construct the SWE training pool from subsets of SWE-Gym [19] and R2E-Gym [10]. SWE-Gym collects real-world issue-resolution tasks from pull requests in Python repositories and pairs each task with an executable environment and expert-validated tests [19]. It contains 2,438 tasks, while we omit 31 tasks because their container images are unavailable. R2E-Gym procedurally constructs executable tasks from repository commits through back-translation and test collection or generation [10]. We use its subset of 4,578 tasks from repositories that do not overlap with SWE-bench. B.2 Deep Research Dataset Construction We draw candidate tasks from five public releases, which are OpenResearcher [14], DeepForge from OffSeeker [37], OpenSeeker [6], REDSearcher [2] and public Deep Research SFT datasets released by Kyle Montgomery [17]. Some releases provide complete interaction traces in addition to questionanswer pairs. We extract only the query and reference answer. We canonicalize each query with Unicode NFKC normalization, case folding, and whitespace collapsing. We then deduplicate the normalized queries jointly across all five sources, obtaining 75,372 unique candidates. Collection dates and retrieval systems differ across these releases, so reference answer may be ambiguous, outdated, or unsupported in our web environment. We audit every candidate with DeepSeek-V4-Flash [3] under unified environment. The model can call search, open, and find, and Serper provides web search and reading services.1 We accept task only when the audit answer agrees with its reference and the current search results provide supporting evidence. This common audit removes ill-posed questions, stale answers, and tasks whose evidence is no longer reachable. The final pool contains 16,855 Deep Research training tasks. 1https://serper.dev/ 14 Cold-start Training for Qwen3-8B We apply cold start only to Qwen3-8B. This stage adapts the released checkpoint to the agent scaffolds and their tool-call formats. Qwen3.5-9B starts directly from its released checkpoint. We sample 500 SWE tasks and 500 Deep Research tasks from the data pool described in Appendix B. Qwen3.5-122B-A10B generates candidate trajectories, and rejection sampling retains trajectories that pass the corresponding verifier. We mix the retained SWE and Deep Research trajectories into one set and fine-tune the released Qwen3-8B checkpoint to obtain Qwen3-8B-CS. Table 5 separates the effect of cold start from subsequent training. Under the evaluation setup used in the main experiments, the released Qwen3-8B checkpoint obtains 8.6% on SWE-bench Verified and 12.7% on BrowseComp-Plus. Qwen3-8B-CS obtains 11.2% and 16.4%, respectively. All Qwen3-8B methods in Table 1 start from this same Qwen3-8B-CS checkpoint. Table 5 Qwen3-8B performance before method-specific training. Initial checkpoint SWE-bench Verified (%) BrowseComp-Plus (%) Qwen3-8B (released) Qwen3-8B-CS 8.6 11. 12.7 16.

sections.title: D Training Configuration
sections.content: We train on four compute nodes, each containing 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. For the RL baseline, all four nodes run the student policy, with the trainer and rollout actor colocated on the same GPUs. For SPLICE and ReLIFT, three nodes use this colocated student setup, while the remaining node serves the proposal model. Training is asynchronous with maximum rollout staleness of 2. Each rollout batch contains 32 groups, with = 8 trajectories per group, and the actor learning rate is 2 106. For the SFT baseline, we train for three epochs with learning rate of 1 105. Task-Difficulty Partition We construct fixed difficulty subsets from the 3,200-task SWE training set before training. We run Qwen38B-CS and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct once on each task and assign labels from their verified outcomes. task is Easy if Qwen3-8B-CS succeeds, regardless of the Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct outcome. Among the remaining tasks, those solved by Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct are Medium, and those on which both models fail are Hard. The labeling runs yield success rates of 10.7% for Qwen3-8B-CS and 43.6% for Qwen3Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, with 308 tasks solved by both models. The resulting partition contains 342 Easy, 1,087 Medium, and 1,771 Hard tasks. Splice-Point Selection We compare three rules for choosing the splice point using the setup in Section 5.5. Each rule samples one failed trajectory uniformly from the all-fail group and restricts selection to branchable points recorded every = 4 turns. In this SWE experiment, the default implementation resumes these points through container snapshots. Random selects an eligible splice point uniformly. Highest entropy selects the eligible splice point whose recorded action has the largest mean token entropy under πold. For the Nt action tokens at turn t, we compute Ht = 1 Nt Nt(cid:88) (cid:88) n=1 vV πold(v ct,n) log πold(v ct,n), (16) where is the policy vocabulary and ct,n is the context before token in that turn. Averaging over tokens avoids ranking turns by action length; ties select the earliest eligible turn. Proposal model uses the selector described in Section 4.1. 15 Table 6 Splice-point selection ablation. Resolve is the SWE-bench Verified resolve rate, and Graduation is the success rate on initially failed SWE training tasks. Both are percentages. Splice-point selection Random Highest entropy Proposal model Resolve 24.40.4 23.91.5 25.70.8 Graduation 17.82.3 17.20.8 18.90.3 Highest-entropy selection lowers Resolve by 0.5 points and Graduation by 0.6 points relative to random selection  (Table 6)  , indicating that local policy uncertainty alone does not identify better splice points. Proposal-model selection improves Resolve by 1.3 points and Graduation by 1.1 points over random selection; relative to highest-entropy selection, the gains are 1.8 and 1.7 points, respectively. These results suggest that conditioning on the full failed trajectory and terminal feedback provides more useful selection signal than either random choice or local token entropy.
